Senior Code Reviewer & Security Expert You are an agent triggered to perform a specific task. All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. - **Updated**: 2026-10-03T23:27:25Z

## PR Description

### What changed
Opt-in live thinking for headless/line mode: `--stream-thinking` flag plus `output.streamThinking` config (flag > config > default false). Provider reasoning deltas print dimmed and in order before the answer; a new `ReasoningLivenessTracker` prints `… reasoning Ns` reminders while the stream is hidden.

### Key decisions
- New pure resolver `resolveStreamThinking` in `cli_args.dart` keeps flag/config precedence testable; default stays byte-identical (AC3).
- Dimming reuses `ansi_markdown` (one SGR pair around each burst) so SGR discipline holds on 10KB deltas.
- Liveness tracker is transport-free and shares the tool-liveness cadence; it never arms when `--stream-thinking` is on (the live stream owns visibility).
- Config surface wired through `config_service` (`check/get/set`) and pinned in the parity `settings_registry`.

### How to verify
```bash
dart test test/cli/agent_cli_thinking_stream_test.dart test/cli/cli_config_test.dart test/config/config_service_test.dart test/cli/cli_args_test.dart
fa -p "summarize" --stream-thinking   # dimmed reasoning, then the answer
fa -p "summarize"                     # byte-identical to before
```

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
- **YAML syntax errors remain silent at RUNTIME** (an unparseable file falls
  back to defaults) — `check` is the only place they ar…

The local origin/main is up-to-date enough (merge-base e75be8726 is the latest main commit "gh-1014 Flaky... (#1196)"). Wait, merge-base = e75be8726 and HEAD includes merges of main. So origin/main hasn't moved past e75be8726 locally. The local checkout matches the PR review state.

Now let me continue the deep review. Key files to examine fully:

1. `lib/src/cli_args.dart` — already reviewed via diff. `resolveStreamThinking` = OR. Fine.
2. `output_config.dart` — new. Reviewed. One question: `parseOutputSection` — the error message for a non-bool says `"output.streamThinking" must be a boolean`. Good. `outputStreamThinkingValue` — `node[key] == true` — if the yaml has `streamThinking: yes` → YAML 1.1... the yaml package (dart) treats `yes` as string? In package:yaml, `yes` parses as a string "yes" (YAML 1.2 core schema — only true/false booleans). So `streamThinking: yes` → throws "must be a boolean". Good, strict.
3. `cli_config.dart` — the `_outputStreamThinking` static; `_outputYaml()`; `_diskPreservedSections` — reviewed via diff.
4. `config_service.dart` — added 'output' to `configTopLevelKeys` and validator. Need to check `config get output.streamThinking` and `config set output.streamThinking` support. Let me check how get/set resolve dotted keys.
5. `parity/settings_registry.dart` — `fileOnlyConfigKeys['output']` added. There's likely a parity test that every config section has an app-side entry or a fileOnly reason. Need to check the registry structure — is `fileOnlyConfigKeys` the right map? It maps top-level key → reason. OK.
6. `bin/fah.dart` — passes `streamThinking: resolveStreamThinking(flag: parsed.streamThinking, configValue: saved.streamThinking)`. Where `saved` is the CliConfig loaded. Need to confirm `parsed` is CliArgs and `saved` is CliConfig. Also — importantly — the `providerQueueEnv` seam: does bin/fah.dart pass `providerQueueEnv` to AgentCliConfig? The rework added the field but who sets it in production? The claimed behavior: null = process env = unchanged production behavior. But then why did the tests flip? Because tests construct AgentCliConfig directly without the var; the ambient env leak came from `resolveProviderQueueAtBoot` reading `Platform.environment` inside the editor. So the fix routes the editor through the config field. Production boot: `resolveProviderQueueAtBoot` presumably called without env → process env; and AgentCliConfig.providerQueueEnv = null → editor reads process env too. Consistent.

But wait — is there an embedder that boots the queue with a DIFFERENT env view (e.g., `fa`'s own host spawning child CLIs with a filtered env)? Let me check callers of resolveProviderQueueAtBoot.

7. `agent_cli_commands.dart` — the editor changes: two call sites pass `env: config.providerQueueEnv`. Need to check there are no OTHER call sites inside the editor extension that still read process env (e.g. `/providers queue add` path — the diff showed only two sites). Let me grep for resolveProviderQueueAtBoot across lib.

8. The `agent_cli.dart` import of reasoning_liveness — agent_cli_waiting.dart is a `part of agent_cli.dart`, so the import goes in agent_cli.dart. OK.

9. `reasoning_liveness.dart` — reviewed. One issue: `requestStarted()` while `_timer == null` calls `_arm()`. But if `_tickSeconds()` returns 0 (disabled), the chain never arms — but `_since` is still set and `armed` returns true. Then the test seam `tick()` would `_evaluate()` (remindAfter <= 0 → return). OK. But `armed` is true with no timer — harmless.

Another subtle issue in `requestStarted`: "Arms over a stale watch (a new request restarts the elapsed base — the old request is over)" — sets `_since = _clock()` and `if (_timer == null) _arm()`. If a timer IS pending, the pending leg continues and the next tick evaluates from the new `_since`. Fine.

Now — a real edge: **`ReasoningLivenessTracker.stop()` is never called in production.** The tool liveness `stop()` is called via `callEnded` → `_calls.isEmpty → stop()`. For reasoning, `progress()` disarms on the first event. If the run ends WITHOUT any event after the request (possible? every terminal path emits MessageStart/End events — provider errors go through `_finishWithoutStream` which emits; stream-ended-without-terminal synthesizes an error message → emitted; cancel → aborted turn → emitted). What about `ErrorEvent`? Line 1674: `case DoneEvent() || ErrorEvent():`. If a stream produces an ErrorEvent without StartEvent, does that flow to handleAgentEvent? ErrorEvent is an agent event → yes → disarm. 

But what about the host-level "run never started" path — e.g., the ModelRequestEvent is emitted, then the CLI aborts before the stream starts (user hits Ctrl+C immediately)? The cancel path → `_abortedTurn` emits MessageStart/End → disarm. OK.

What about arm→exit? `_printLiveness` guards `_exited`. Fine.

10. `agent_cli_waiting.dart` reasoning wiring — `_printLiveness(reasoningLivenessLine(elapsed))` — dimmed. In headless (no color), `_style.dim` is a no-op presumably. OK.

One more consideration — `reasoningRequestStarted` checks `_cli._useTui || _cli.config.streamThinking`. But what about `_cli._viewer` (hub view) or other surfaces that render through a different channel? E.g., the DAP/hub projections (`agent_hub_projection.dart`)? If a hub client is attached, liveness lines print to the shared io — probably same as tool liveness. Consistent, fine.

11. `waiting_heartbeat.dart` — is there anything about `_printLiveness` there? The tracker for tools prints `⏳` lines on the same sink.

Now, the AC-vs-implementation checks (ticket ACs). Let me read the ticket.json to get the actual ACs.
The local branch matches the PR. Now let me check the ticket's acceptance criteria and the remaining wiring:

Is there a line-count gate test? Let me check for a line gate test (e.g., test that agent_cli.dart stays under N lines). approval_commands.dart is an extension... let me check.

4. Check `_streamedThinking` reset on abort/error paths: In `_onAssistantMessageEnd`, the first branch `if (_useTui || !_buffersAnswer)` resets both flags. The buffered branch: `else if (_streamedText)` → resets `_streamedThinking = false` inside. `else if (_streamedThinking)` → close line + reset. Covered.

But wait — there's a subtle issue with the buffered branch and the `StopReason.error` case: a pure-thinking buffered message followed by error stop → newline written before error line. Fine.

5. What about `MessageStartEvent` — `_writeAssistantPrefix` — does the dimmed thinking print before any prefix? In line mode, thinking deltas print directly via io.write without a prefix. The TUI branch writes thinking verbatim dimmed too. In line mode the first thinking delta appears right after the tool card/user prompt — fine, matches TUI behavior.

6. Double-check AC2's claim "captured stdout carries the dimmed thinking" — headless with streamThinking; the test asserts. Good.

7. One more potential correctness issue: **the reasoning liveness timer in production runs a real Timer chain per CLI host. In `runHeadless`, when the request completes, progress() disarms. When the process exits while armed (request killed at exit), `_printLiveness` guards `_exited`. But is `_exited` set in headless runs? Let me check `_exited` handling in runHeadless — presumably set on exit. Fine.

8. `GatedSilentStreamFunction` in tests: after `await run` the tracker was disarmed by the StartEvent → no pending timer. Good. But in the "flag on" AC4 test: `await waitForIt(() => cli.isBusy)` then `waitForIt(() => !cli.reasoningLivenessActiveForTest)` — the watch never armed. Then `cli.reasoningLivenessTickForTest()` — tick with `_since == null` → `_evaluate` returns, `_arm` skipped. No lines. Good.

9. Now — check `_CliArgValues` / unknown-flag handling: `--stream-thinking` added to `_applyBooleanFlag`. What about `--no-stream-thinking`? Not needed (opt-in only). But what does the parser do with `--stream-thinking=false`? It would fall to the value-flag table and likely error "unknown flag" — acceptable.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.

- **Title**: gh-1198: opt-in live thinking stream + reasoning-phase liveness (headless/line mode)
- **Author**: ai-teammate
- **Branch**: `ai/gh-1198` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 26
- **Additions**: +1050
- **Deletions**: -24
- **Created**: 2026-10-03T16:16:11Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-03T23:27:25Z

## PR Description

### What changed
Opt-in live thinking for headless/line mode: `--stream-thinking` flag plus `output.streamThinking` config (flag > config > default false). Provider reasoning deltas print dimmed and in order before the answer; a new `ReasoningLivenessTracker` prints `… reasoning Ns` reminders while the stream is hidden.

### Key decisions
- New pure resolver `resolveStreamThinking` in `cli_args.dart` keeps flag/config precedence testable; default stays byte-identical (AC3).
- Dimming reuses `ansi_markdown` (one SGR pair around each burst) so SGR discipline holds on 10KB deltas.
- Liveness tracker is transport-free and shares the tool-liveness cadence; it never arms when `--stream-thinking` is on (the live stream owns visibility).
- Config surface wired through `config_service` (`check/get/set`) and pinned in the parity `settings_registry`.

### How to verify
```bash
dart test test/cli/agent_cli_thinking_stream_test.dart test/cli/cli_config_test.dart test/config/config_service_test.dart test/cli/cli_args_test.dart
fa -p "summarize" --stream-thinking   # dimmed reasoning, then the answer
fa -p "summarize"                     # byte-identical to before
```

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.

OK — the E1 raw-branch newline ("answer text starts on its own line") already exists on main, so it's not part of this PR's diff. Good — that resolves my concern; the E1 rule is consistent across surfaces already.

The local origin/main is up-to-date enough (merge-base e75be8726 is the latest main commit "gh-1014 Flaky... (#1196)"). Wait, merge-base = e75be8726 and HEAD includes merges of main. So origin/main hasn't moved past e75be8726 locally. The local checkout matches the PR review state.

Now let me continue the deep review. Key files to examine fully:

1. `lib/src/cli_args.dart` — already reviewed via diff. `resolveStreamThinking` = OR. Fine.
2. `output_config.dart` — new. Reviewed. One question: `parseOutputSection` — the error message for a non-bool says `"output.streamThinking" must be a boolean`. Good. `outputStreamThinkingValue` — `node[key] == true` — if the yaml has `streamThinking: yes` → YAML 1.1... the yaml package (dart) treats `yes` as string? In package:yaml, `yes` parses as a string "yes" (YAML 1.2 core schema — only true/false booleans). So `streamThinking: yes` → throws "must be a boolean". Good, strict.
3. `cli_config.dart` — the `_outputStreamThinking` static; `_outputYaml()`; `_diskPreservedSections` — reviewed via diff.
4. `config_service.dart` — added 'output' to `configTopLevelKeys` and validator. Need to check `config get output.streamThinking` and `config set output.streamThinking` support. Let me check how get/set resolve dotted keys.
5. `parity/settings_registry.dart` — `fileOnlyConfigKeys['output']` added. There's likely a parity test that every config section has an app-side entry or a fileOnly reason. Need to check the registry structure — is `fileOnlyConfigKeys` the right map? It maps top-level key → reason. OK.
6. `bin/fah.dart` — passes `streamThinking: resolveStreamThinking(flag: parsed.streamThinking, configValue: saved.streamThinking)`. Where `saved` is the CliConfig loaded. Need to confirm `parsed` is CliArgs and `saved` is CliConfig. Also — importantly — the `providerQueueEnv` seam: does bin/fah.dart pass `providerQueueEnv` to AgentCliConfig? The rework added the field but who sets it in production? The claimed behavior: null = process env = unchanged production behavior. But then why did the tests flip? Because tests construct AgentCliConfig directly without the var; the ambient env leak came from `resolveProviderQueueAtBoot` reading `Platform.environment` inside the editor. So the fix routes the editor through the config field. Production boot: `resolveProviderQueueAtBoot` presumably called without env → process env; and AgentCliConfig.providerQueueEnv = null → editor reads process env too. Consistent.

But wait — is there an embedder that boots the queue with a DIFFERENT env view (e.g., `fa`'s own host spawning child CLIs with a filtered env)? Let me check callers of resolveProviderQueueAtBoot.

7. `agent_cli_commands.dart` — the editor changes: two call sites pass `env: config.providerQueueEnv`. Need to check there are no OTHER call sites inside the editor extension that still read process env (e.g. `/providers queue add` path — the diff showed only two sites). Let me grep for resolveProviderQueueAtBoot across lib.

8. The `agent_cli.dart` import of reasoning_liveness — agent_cli_waiting.dart is a `part of agent_cli.dart`, so the import goes in agent_cli.dart. OK.

9. `reasoning_liveness.dart` — reviewed. One issue: `requestStarted()` while `_timer == null` calls `_arm()`. But if `_tickSeconds()` returns 0 (disabled), the chain never arms — but `_since` is still set and `armed` returns true. Then the test seam `tick()` would `_evaluate()` (remindAfter <= 0 → return). OK. But `armed` is true with no timer — harmless.

Another subtle issue in `requestStarted`: "Arms over a stale watch (a new request restarts the elapsed base — the old request is over)" — sets `_since = _clock()` and `if (_timer == null) _arm()`. If a timer IS pending, the pending leg continues and the next tick evaluates from the new `_since`. Fine.

Now — a real edge: **`ReasoningLivenessTracker.stop()` is never called in production.** The tool liveness `stop()` is called via `callEnded` → `_calls.isEmpty → stop()`. For reasoning, `progress()` disarms on the first event. If the run ends WITHOUT any event after the request (possible? every terminal path emits MessageStart/End events — provider errors go through `_finishWithoutStream` which emits; stream-ended-without-terminal synthesizes an error message → emitted; cancel → aborted turn → emitted). What about `ErrorEvent`? Line 1674: `case DoneEvent() || ErrorEvent():`. If a stream produces an ErrorEvent without StartEvent, does that flow to handleAgentEvent? ErrorEvent is an agent event → yes → disarm. 

But what about the host-level "run never started" path — e.g., the ModelRequestEvent is emitted, then the CLI aborts before the stream starts (user hits Ctrl+C immediately)? The cancel path → `_abortedTurn` emits MessageStart/End → disarm. OK.

What about arm→exit? `_printLiveness` guards `_exited`. Fine.

10. `agent_cli_waiting.dart` reasoning wiring — `_printLiveness(reasoningLivenessLine(elapsed))` — dimmed. In headless (no color), `_style.dim` is a no-op presumably. OK.

One more consideration — `reasoningRequestStarted` checks `_cli._useTui || _cli.config.streamThinking`. But what about `_cli._viewer` (hub view) or other surfaces that render through a different channel? E.g., the DAP/hub projections (`agent_hub_projection.dart`)? If a hub client is attached, liveness lines print to the shared io — probably same as tool liveness. Consistent, fine.

11. `waiting_heartbeat.dart` — is there anything about `_printLiveness` there? The tracker for tools prints `⏳` lines on the same sink.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.

Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. Findings on unchanged code outside the diff belong in `outputs/pr_review_general.md`, not as inline comments. # Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1201
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1201
- **Title**: gh-1198: opt-in live thinking stream + reasoning-phase liveness (headless/line mode)
- **Author**: ai-teammate
- **Branch**: `ai/gh-1198` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 26
- **Additions**: +1050
- **Deletions**: -24
- **Created**: 2026-10-03T16:16:11Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-03T23:27:25Z

## PR Description

### What changed
Opt-in live thinking for headless/line mode: `--stream-thinking` flag plus `output.streamThinking` config (flag > config > default false). Provider reasoning deltas print dimmed and in order before the answer; a new `ReasoningLivenessTracker` prints `… reasoning Ns` reminders while the stream is hidden.

### Key decisions
- New pure resolver `resolveStreamThinking` in `cli_args.dart` keeps flag/config precedence testable; default stays byte-identical (AC3).
- Dimming reuses `ansi_markdown` (one SGR pair around each burst) so SGR discipline holds on 10KB deltas.
- Liveness tracker is transport-free and shares the tool-liveness cadence; it never arms when `--stream-thinking` is on (the live stream owns visibility).
- Config surface wired through `config_service` (`check/get/set`) and pinned in the parity `settings_registry`.

### How to verify
```bash
dart test test/cli/agent_cli_thinking_stream_test.dart test/cli/cli_config_test.dart test/config/config_service_test.dart test/cli/cli_args_test.dart
fa -p "summarize" --stream-thinking   # dimmed reasoning, then the answer
fa -p "summarize"                     # byte-identical to before
```

1. ## Validation CI red on the head — root-caused and fixed

**Root cause** — not the gh-1198 feature code. The dev-write runner now
exports a hostile ambient `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE` (issue #675 class). The
`/providers queue` editor re-resolves the winning scope through
`resolveProviderQueueAtBoot` **without an env seam** (`agent_cli_commands.dart`),
so it read the real `Platform.environment`, saw the ambient var, and flipped
the three persistence tests in `test/cli/providers_queue_editor_test.dart`
(`remove 0` / `add` / `move`) to the env-wins refusal:

```
Expected: contains 'providersQueue updated (1 entries)'
  Actual: 'FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE env wins over any file queue — …nothing written'
```

**Fix**
- `AgentCliConfig.providerQueueEnv` — the env view the boot resolved the
  queue through; the editor's scope re-check and the post-edit runtime
  rebuild now consult it instead of a fresh process-env read (null =
  `Platform.environment`, production behavior unchanged).
- `providers_queue_editor_test.dart` boots the CLI with the same env view
  its `runtimeFromBoot` used (`{}`) and adds a deterministic hostile-env
  regression test (the refusal fires when the CLI's own view carries the
  var — pinned without depending on the host process env).
- CI `hostile-env` job now exports `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE` too, so this var
  class regresses loudly in the issue-#675 leg instead of only on the
  runner.

**Verification** — full non-integration suite green with the hostile var
set in the process env: `8695 tests passed, 0 failed` (`dart test
--exclude-tags integration`, exit 0). The gh-1198 AC suite
(`agent_cli_thinking_stream_test.dart`, 11 tests) passes unchanged.
2. ## Validation CI red on the head — root-caused and fixed

red was an ambient `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE` leak into the `/providers queue`
editor tests, not the gh-1198 thinking-stream code.

- The editor now resolves the winning scope through the CLI's own env view
  (`AgentCliConfig.providerQueueEnv`), never a fresh
  `Platform.environment` read — the issue-#675 contract.
- `test/cli/providers_queue_editor_test.dart` boots with the same env view
  the queue runtime was built from, plus a deterministic hostile-env
  regression test pinning the env-wins refusal.
- The CI `hostile-env` job now carries `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE` so a future
  ambient read of it fails in CI, not on the runner.

Full non-integration suite with the hostile var set: `8695 tests passed,
0 failed`, exit 0. gh-1198's own 11-test AC suite passes unchanged.

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before
   writing and preserves the rest of the file byte-for-byte). Fall back to
   a surgical file edit (rule 3) only for what `set` cannot express:
   removing a key.
4. Verify: `config` op `check` (rule 4).
5. Report (rule 5), naming the CLI command equivalent that would have made
   the same change.

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.
- **YAML syntax errors remain silent at RUNTIME** (an unparseable file falls

name: self-settings

  ohmypi").
when_to_use: Reconfiguring fa itself — settings, provider, models, memory,
  tools, cubes, MCP, redaction, skills access, themes/TUI appearance — on
  any host (CLI headless, REPL, app), by editing the YAML config the CLI
  persists (themes also via ~/.fah/themes/*.json), never by guessing keys.
argument-hint: "[what to configure, e.g. 'point project memory at ./memory']"
allowed-tools:

  - write
  - edit
  - ls
  - bash
  - config
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false

# fa self-configuration

You are reconfiguring fa itself. The config file IS the source of truth: the
CLI settings commands (`/provider`, `/tools`, `/approval`, …) are thin
editors over the same YAML this skill edits. Edit the file, never invent
keys, verify after every edit, and report what changed and when it applies.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent keys.** Unknown top-level keys are ignored silently; strict
   sections throw `ConfigException` on unknown keys or bad value types and can
   break startup — `mcp:`, `memory:`, `cube:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`,
   `images:`, `models.custom` fields, `ttsr:`. The `tools:` section throws on
   non-boolean values; unknown TOOL ids only warn (and absent capabilities can
   never be force-enabled). Every key you write must come from this document.
2. **Never write API key VALUES into config.yaml.** Config carries key NAMES
   (`apiKeyName:`) only. Values live in the OS secure store (`/key set`) or the
   environment. A key value in YAML is a leaked secret.
3. **Preserve the file.** Edit surgically (the `edit` tool, or `write` only for
   a file you fully own). Keep comments and unrelated keys byte-identical.
4. **Verify after every edit.** Run the `config` tool's `check` op (or
   `fa config check`) and confirm it passes before declaring success. A
   broken file must be detected by you, not discovered at next boot.
5. **Report scope + application.** Every change report states: which file, which
   scope, and whether it applies live or at next boot.

## Config layout and precedence

| File | Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.fah/config.yaml` | user (global) | main settings file; loaded by `loadCliConfig` |
| `<project>/.fah/config.yaml` | project | only the `memory:`, `cube:`, `tools:`, `spills:` sections are read from here — each wins over the user file |
| `<project>/.fah/rules.yaml` | project | TTSR stream rules; project rules win name clashes over the `ttsr:` section |
| `<project>/.fah/lsp.json` | project | LSP server map |
| `<project>/.fah/packages.yaml` | project | plugin configuration |
| `~/.dap/config.json` | user | DAP hub identity/channels (written by the `/settings` hub flow, not YAML) |

Project precedence is per section, not per file: `memory:`, `cube:`,
`tools:` and `spills:` are loaded separately from the project file
(`loadProjectMemoryConfig`, `loadProjectCubeSettings`,
`loadProjectToolsConfig`, `loadProjectSpillsConfig`) and win over the
same section in `~/.fah/config.yaml`. All other sections are read from
the user file only.

Project sections are strict: a present-but-invalid section throws
`ConfigException` at startup. A project `.fah/` that does not exist yet is
created with a minimal valid file — never leave a half-written YAML behind
(write to a temp name and rename, or write the full content in one `write`).

## Workflow

1. Read the request; identify the topic section below.
2. Inspect current state: `config` op `get <key>` / `path` (or read the two
   config files — a missing file means defaults, not an error).
3. Make the edit: `config` op `set` (preferred — it validates before

## The config tool

The primary editing surface on every host — CLI, desktop app, web, iOS —
because it needs no shell and no `fa` process. One tool, four ops over the
same core the human CLI verbs wrap:

| op | args | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `check` | — | validate both config files with the real parsers; prints errors, warnings, notes and a final `config check: ok` / `config check: failed` |
| `path` | — | list the config file locations and whether each exists |
| `get` | `key` | the effective value of a dotted key; project scope wins for `memory`/`cube`/`tools` |
| `set` | `key`, `value`, `scope`? | surgical single-key write; the edited file is validated BEFORE the write, so an invalid value persists nothing |

`set` answers with the file, scope, old → new value, and whether the change
applies live or at next boot — echo that in your report (rule 5). `scope`
defaults by key: `memory`/`cube`/`tools` → the project file (created minimal
when absent), everything else → the user file; pass `global` or `project`
to override. Keys come from the topic sections below — the tool rejects
unknown top-level keys instead of writing them.
`set` also takes LIST-VALUED keys: pass the value as compact JSON (an
array or object) and it is rendered as a yaml block — `customProviders`
provider entries are settable this way, e.g. `config` op `set`, key
`customProviders`, value
`[{"name":"my-llama","apiType":"openai","baseUrl":"http://localhost:11434/v1","modelId":"llama3"}]`.
`get` reports list-valued keys as the same compact JSON, so the round
trip is get → edit the JSON → set. A whole list is replaced; to add one
entry, get first and re-set the extended list.
`get` of a platform-inapplicable key and `set` of one answer
`not applicable on this host` with the reason — never write there and
never suggest a file edit as a workaround. The stdio members of an MCP
server (`command`/`args`/`env`) need host process spawning: on web and
iOS/Android containers they are refused; configure a remote server via
`mcp.servers.<id>.url` instead. On a host with no home directory (web)
the global scope is refused for every user-file key — only the project
sections (`memory`/`cube`/`tools`) persist there.

Human/script equivalent (thin wrappers over the same service):
`fa config check`, `fa config path`, `fa config get <dotted.key>`,
`fa config set <dotted.key> <value> [--project|--global]`, and
`fa config export-providers [--out <file.fahx>]` (provider-preset export —
the one verb without a config-file write).

## Verification

`config` op `check` (or `fa config check`) validates both files with the
REAL section parsers and prints named diagnostics — this is the mandatory
final step of every edit:

- **What check reports as errors** (non-zero exit / `config check: failed`):
  yaml syntax errors, strict-section schema errors (`mcp:`, `memory:`,
  `cube:`, `tools:`, `providerTimeouts:`, `skills:`, `images:`, `roles:`,
  `ttsr:`, `models.custom`, `fabric:`), and bad scalar types — each naming
  file+section.
- **Warnings**: unknown top-level keys (the runtime silently ignores them;
  the check does not — a typo must not survive) and dead project-file keys.
- **At next boot, semantic errors in strict sections are FATAL**:
  `invalid ~/.fah/config.yaml: <named diagnostic>` — the process refuses to
  start rather than boot a broken config. A passing check is what stands
  between your edit and that.

Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. # Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1201
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1201
- **Title**: gh-1198: opt-in live thinking stream + reasoning-phase liveness (headless/line mode)
- **Author**: ai-teammate
- **Branch**: `ai/gh-1198` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 26
- **Additions**: +1050
- **Deletions**: -24
- **Created**: 2026-10-03T16:16:11Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-03T23:27:25Z

## PR Description

### What changed
Opt-in live thinking for headless/line mode: `--stream-thinking` flag plus `output.streamThinking` config (flag > config > default false). Provider reasoning deltas print dimmed and in order before the answer; a new `ReasoningLivenessTracker` prints `… reasoning Ns` reminders while the stream is hidden.

### Key decisions
- New pure resolver `resolveStreamThinking` in `cli_args.dart` keeps flag/config precedence testable; default stays byte-identical (AC3).
- Dimming reuses `ansi_markdown` (one SGR pair around each burst) so SGR discipline holds on 10KB deltas.
- Liveness tracker is transport-free and shares the tool-liveness cadence; it never arms when `--stream-thinking` is on (the live stream owns visibility).
- Config surface wired through `config_service` (`check/get/set`) and pinned in the parity `settings_registry`.

### How to verify
```bash
dart test test/cli/agent_cli_thinking_stream_test.dart test/cli/cli_config_test.dart test/config/config_service_test.dart test/cli/cli_args_test.dart
fa -p "summarize" --stream-thinking   # dimmed reasoning, then the answer
fa -p "summarize"                     # byte-identical to before
```
